_note: The Tanbark Road's people (decision 0427): the Rowes at the bark shed, Lydia Fairbanks and her three in the Mast Wood, Jotham Leavitt and his wagon, Jasper at the Hemlock Wall. Voices from docs/regions/tanbark-road.md. Draft lines, for Matt or his writer friend.

lines.text: An old man works a spud down a hemlock log. The bark comes away in one long curl, and he lays it on the rick without looking.
Morning. Road's open, if you're going down. Nobody much comes up.
We're going down.
Then mind the woods after dark. Not for anything in them. You'll hear him, is all.
Hear who?
Fiddle. Up in the hemlocks, most nights. Same tune every time. Sad one.
Fiddles don't hurt anybody.
No. They don't.
Mrs. Applegate looks south down the road, and keeps looking.
Wagon comes once a month now. When it comes. Tannery's buying less.
Shame about the trees. Good timber, standing there dead.
Wasn't the timber they wanted, Thayer. It was the bark.
She chalks a mark on the end of a rick, counts under her breath, and chalks another.
Forty-one. Don't make me lose it.
Your husband says there's a fiddler in the woods.
The Night Man. That's what we call him. Folk down the hill say ghost. He's no ghost.
We leave the cup full at the spring. It's empty by morning.
Forty-four. Forty-five.
I knew whose girl it was. That went missing.
Whose?
Poor soul. He's not a joke up here, whatever he is in town.
She doesn't say his name.
A woman in a town shawl is filling sacks with beechnuts, fast, while three children do something more like eating them.
Mast year. Every squirrel in the county's out, and every widow. Ned, those are for selling.
Mister, there's a ghost in these woods. It plays the fiddle and it screams.
It's the lost girl. From the Bridge. She's calling for her father.
That's enough.
She says it hard, and the children go quiet. Sam goes on eating.
Beechnuts sell at the square, Thursdays. Acorns are for the pig.
The screaming in the woods at night. It was a catamount.
Well. Don't tell Ned. He'll be sorry it wasn't a ghost.
I'm sorry about the children. They hear things and they say them.
He sang at my wedding. Best voice in the county. Folk forget that.
If you hear it, don't follow it. That's how it gets you.
How does it get you?
I don't know. Nobody's ever come back to say.
Ned says it's a ghost. Is it a ghost?
I've never met one.
That's what a ghost would say.
Sam holds up a beechnut, considers it, and eats it.
A big man in a canvas coat is standing by an empty bark wagon, rubbing the back of his neck, and looking up the road.
Leavitt. Tannery wagon. I'd be up at the Rowes' by now, if not for him.
He nods down the road. Something very large is standing on it.
Bull moose. In the rut. Takes anything tall for a rival, and the horses won't go past.
The bull of the woods.
That's what the Rowes call him. They think it's very funny. It's a word for the camp boss, up north.
Two days I've sat here. The horses don't like it. I don't like it.
Well. That's the road clear.
Here. It's not much, but it's warm, and it's been up and down this road more than I have.
He takes off his coat, shakes it, and hands it over. It smells of horse and hemlock.
I'll be down at the Bridge before you, likely. Ask at the tannery if you need a ride back up.
Polly dropped a sack somewhere back in the big beeches and won't go after it. Not with the noise that moose makes.
It was the ghost.
It was the moose. If you're passing that way.
Deep in the beeches, west of the road. A sack with a red string on it.
That's the one. Polly, say thank you.
Was it the ghost?
It was a sack.
Here. It was my mother's, for the nutting. Six pockets, and I've never got the last beechnut out of any of them.
